items.title: AI and complements
items.summary:
In a “weak links” model of production, where tasks are complements, the gains from automation tend to arrive slowly because output is constrained by the least productive tasks. But the same complementarity makes attacks more harmful and easier to execute. For example, with an elasticity of substitution across tasks of 0.2, automating tasks worth 1 percent of GDP with a tenfold increase in productivity raises output by less than one percent, while cutting their productivity tenfold lowers output by 68 percent on impact. Whena larger AI sector simultaneously makes AI models more capable and attacks more likely, the positive productivity spillover is negligible compared with the potential damage, so the market overinvests in AI. In a weak-link economy, the costs and benefits from AI can be extremely asymmetric.

That is from a recent “in progress” manuscript by Charles I. Jones and Christopher Tonetti.  Via Lukas Freund .

The post AI and complements appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Privatize Air Traffic Control, Redux
items.summary:
Yesterday the FAA grounded every domestic departure in the United States for more than four hours. Such groundings appear to be happening more often. The last nationwide grounding was in 2023, and regional ones have hit Newark, Dallas, and the entire Northeast in the past two years.

My post from October of 2025 (below) was prompted by regional groundings and delays caused by labor problems. Air traffic control was then (and still is today) far understaffed, and then, absurdly, the government shutdown hit the controllers we had, thus further stressing the system. According to Transportation Secretary Duffy the cause of yesterday’s grounding wasn’t labor but capital: aging TDM telecom circuits overloaded with data.

The deeper cause is the same in both cases: poor incentives. Airlines bear the costs when the system fails and have almost no say in how it is run. By the way, some will crow that yesterday’s failure may have been due to a private contractor. That may well be true–Pro tip: Do not update system software on a Friday at 3pm–but it is beside the point. Contracting out may have some advantages, especially if there is competition, but it is not the same as privatization. The argument for privatization of air traffic control services is to give responsibility for the system to the people who pay when it fails. Align incentives.

My 2025 post. No indent.

Yesterday, the FAA grounded flights at Reagan (DCA) because there weren’t enough air traffic controllers. By mid‑afternoon, thousands of flights were delayed nationwide. The same thing is happening at major airports…
items.t: Privatize Air Traffic Control, Redux

items.title: People like their jobs, even British people
items.summary: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original “Work Values” Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job—valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI…
items.t: People like their jobs, even British people

items.title: The Power and Roots of Aspirations
items.summary:
Aspirations have become a common theme in empirical economics studies but there is no unified understanding of the range of outcomes they influence, the factors that shape them, and how to measure them. We survey this growing literature. We argue that there is compelling evidence to consider aspirations as a useful lens to analyze human behavior and development outcomes, at the individual and aggregate levels, in poorer and richer countries. The empirical evidence aligns with the theory that high aspirations can lead individuals to achieve better educational, labor market, and other outcomes and can contribute to making countries more equal and prosperous. The empirical evidence also confirms that the mix of social and circumstantial factors shaping aspirations tends to hinder the aspirations of the disadvantaged—such as the poor, immigrants, and women—and can contribute to vicious circles of poverty, high inequality, low social mobility, and low growth. However, high aspirations should not be considered an end in themselves as they can backfire, with deleterious effects, if unmatched with opportunities. Further, we argue that definitional and measurement issues can affect the understanding of the topic and that studies should more explicitly describe their measures of aspirations to ensure that divergent underlying concepts are not mistaken.

That is from a 2025 paper by  Anna Fruttero ,  Noël Muller , and  Óscar Calvo-González.  And here is a 2026 paper on similar topics.

The post The Power and Roots of Aspirations appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: The Power and Roots of Aspirations

items.title: Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion?
items.summary:
From Luis Garicano and Alex Imas :

Hence AI capabilities improved 1.91 times faster after October 2025, but R&D spending grew 6.19 times and the technical workforce 3.10 times. So measured capability gains per dollar fell by approximately 69%, and measured gains per technical employee-year decreased by 38%. These figures are accounting; nothing causal can be inferred…

The accounting exercise we just did cannot tell us which. It shows that returns per dollar decreased: spending multiplied by 6.2 and the pace of progress by 1.9. But two different causes for this are possible. One is congestion: the effort is getting less productive as it increases, because it is hard organizationally to increase the budget by more than five times in a year. The other possibility is that each advance is harder than the last. With enough congestion, these same two numbers are even consistent with each advance making the next one easier, which is what an explosion requires. To know whether a break is needed, we must know what an unchanged relationship would have delivered…

In sum our finding is consistent with that of Bloom and his coauthors: ideas are getting harder to find in AI too, and maintaining the rate of improvement requires ever larger increases in inputs.

Overall the idea of an intelligence explosion still remains to be demonstrated.

The post Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion?

US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

items.title: The Economics of Rent Controls
items.summary:
I appear on Ryan Bourne’s excellent new podcast, The Economics of It . We discuss The Economics of Rent Controls drawing on my essay, Rent Control: The Ceiling Trap . It’s a very good discussion. Here’s one bit (edited slightly to remove some ums for reading and to fix a date I got wrong from memory):

RB: And in your essay you talk about some like truly insane ways that people are trying to signal to landlords that they’ll be good tenants in Oslo. I know you talk about that example.

Tabarrok: Yeah, so in Oslo they had rent controls for many years, but then they got rid of them in 1982 (fixed, AT), And there’s a great paper by Are Oust who looks at what happened. When the rent controls were in place, amazingly he found just like Friedman and Stigler found in San Francisco in 1906 that in Oslo the renters advertised I need an apartment, okay? Won’t you rent me an apartment? And as part of their advertisement they would say I’m willing to look after your cat, I’m willing to, you know, shovel the snow.

And on the other side the landlords would say, well, I’m looking for a good Christian. Uh you know, I’m looking for a uh a heterosexual, you know, single-family couple, whatever—these kinds of things. Sometimes literally advertised, sometimes this would happen, under the table. Um there would be things like you would have to pay uh months–sometimes years–you have to pay your rent years in advance. You know, all kinds of ways in which because of the shortage of apartments, it was the renters who had to advertise…

Even companies would say I’ve got a great employee. Please…
items.t: The Economics of Rent Controls

items.title: Do not overrate zero-sum status-seeking
items.summary:
If people really preferred relatively higher income in a poorer society, then those born in Western Europe and the US would be saving up their money so they could live like kings in Africa. Very few people of middle- or upper-class status in poor countries would try to get to the West. Obviously, what we observe is precisely the opposite. Doctors from Africa will come to America in order to drive a cab if their license to practice medicine isn’t recognized. Research on Middle Eastern and African migrants to Europe shows that they aren’t the poorest of the poor, but are relatively well off for where they come from. There are a lot of stories about how terribly South Asian migrant workers are treated in the Arab Gulf, but this causes no problem in recruiting laborers who want to earn a higher income.

Here is more from Richard Hanania .

items.title: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
items.summary:
‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’

Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

items.t: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
